article.headline: A Fifteen-Layer Map of the AI Supply Chain's Real Chokepoints
article.lede: A retail investor's weekend project — a 15-layer visualization of the AI hardware supply chain, mapping market share and AI-revenue concentration for every bottleneck company from silica mines to fab equipment — illustrates both the appeal and the difficulty of picking supply-chain stocks on the premise that artificial general intelligence is arriving faster than most experts thought possible even five years ago. The chart, posted to X by @_Lonis_, is earnest and more rigorous than most retail financial commentary. It also has a structural problem: the companies it depicts are real, but the actual 2025 production chokepoints sit in layers the visualization either understates or omits entirely.
article.body:
The investment thesis behind the chart rests on *AGI timelines* — probabilistic estimates of when AI systems will reach or surpass human-professional-level performance across cognitive tasks. Those estimates have compressed dramatically: median expert forecasts have collapsed from roughly 2060–2070 a decade ago to approximately 2033 today, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei publicly citing 2027 at Davos 2026 and Microsoft (MSFT) AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman describing human-level performance on most professional tasks as 12–18 months away. Compressed timelines directly justify accelerated infrastructure capex — more data centers, more chips, more copper, more power — and that surge in demand ripples backward through every layer of the supply chain, which is exactly what the chart attempts to trace.

The chart's opening layer covers raw commodities: platinum-group metals via Sibanye-Stillwater (SBSW), rare earth oxides from MP Materials (MP), lithium from Albemarle (ALB), copper from Freeport-McMoRan (FCX), and nickel from Sumitomo Metal Mining (5713.T). Of these, copper is the most directly relevant. S&P Global (SPGI) projects data center copper demand to roughly double by 2040, and hyperscale AI facilities require roughly 30 tonnes of copper per megawatt of installed capacity — a figure that makes Freeport, the world's largest publicly traded copper producer, the strongest case in this layer. The rest are second-order at best. Sibanye is primarily an automotive-cycle palladium-and-platinum story; Albemarle supplies lithium for EV batteries and grid storage — useful for powering data centers, but a long way from a chip. MP Materials' rare earth oxide feeds permanent magnets in data-center cooling fans and robotics, but the company remained loss-making on an operating basis through most of 2025. The chart assigns AI revenue percentages in the 6–10% range across these commodities — a speculative overlay rather than a disclosed segment from any of their filings.

The second layer, wafers and substrates, comes closer to the action. Shin-Etsu Chemical (4063.T) and SUMCO (3436.T) together control roughly 55% of global *300mm silicon wafer* supply — the foundational discs on which every advanced chip is fabricated. SUMCO paid dearly for expansion: depreciation jumped from ¥35 billion to ¥100 billion annually, driving a net loss in 2025 even as leading-edge wafer volumes grew 16% year-on-year. The sharper story in this layer is **ABF substrates** — ultrathin insulating layers that route electrical signals from a chip die to the circuit board. Ibiden (4062.T) and Unimicron (3037.TW) are the only two manufacturers with process capability for the most advanced AI accelerator substrates; Ibiden supplies Nvidia (NVDA) H100 and B200 chips directly. A supply-demand gap for ABF is already forming — projected at 10% by the second half of 2026, widening to 42% by 2028. Behind these substrate makers sits a near-total monopoly most investors have never heard of: Ajinomoto (2802.T), a Japanese food conglomerate, holds roughly 98% of the global market for the ABF film material itself.

The visualization's structural limitation is one of layer selection. The real 2025 production chokepoints — identified by Epoch AI's supply-chain analysis — sit in layers the chart either understates or omits. ***CoWoS*** (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate), Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's (TSM) *advanced packaging* process that integrates logic dies with stacked memory, is essentially a single-source capacity constraint: the four largest AI chip buyers consumed over 90% of global CoWoS output in 2025 while accounting for only 12% of advanced logic-die production. *HBM* (high-bandwidth memory) — the stacked memory that gives AI accelerators their data throughput — is dominated by SK Hynix (000660.KS), Samsung Electronics (005930.KS), and Micron Technology (MU); the shortage extends beyond 2026. A supply-chain map built to identify the next ASML (ASML) — the Dutch company holding a 100% share of *EUV* lithography equipment, without which no leading-edge chip can be manufactured — should weight these layers most heavily.

There is a harder epistemological problem embedded in the exercise. Even granting compressed AGI timelines, which layer of the supply chain captures the most value is not obvious. History suggests that enabling-technology monopolies — ASML (ASML) with its EUV machines, Ajinomoto (2802.T) with its ABF film — often retain more margin than commodity suppliers even when commodity volumes surge. ASML reported €32.7 billion in 2025 revenue at a 52.8% gross margin and has raised 2026 guidance to €36–40 billion on AI-driven demand. Whether raw-materials plays belong in an AGI-timeline portfolio depends on a second-order bet: that the infrastructure buildout will outpace the commodity market's ability to respond with new supply. For copper, that bet has some merit; for palladium, far less.

concepts.definition: Probabilistic estimates of when artificial general intelligence — AI capable of matching or exceeding human-professional-level performance across most cognitive tasks — will be achieved. These estimates have collapsed from a median of roughly 2060–2070 a decade ago to approximately 2033 today, a compression that directly drives accelerated investment in AI infrastructure.

IC substrates made using Ajinomoto Build-up Film, an ultrathin insulating material that routes electrical signals from a chip die's microscopic bond pads out to the larger traces of a circuit board. Advanced AI accelerator chips require high-layer-count ABF substrates with extremely fine line resolution; Ajinomoto holds roughly 98% of the global market for the film itself, making it an invisible monopoly upstream of the substrate makers.

An advanced packaging process developed and produced exclusively by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, in which a logic die and high-bandwidth memory stacks are integrated side-by-side on a shared silicon interposer before being mounted on the final package substrate. CoWoS dramatically increases memory bandwidth and is a prerequisite for high-performance AI training chips; TSMC is currently the sole commercial source at leading-edge specifications.

A type of DRAM in which multiple memory dies are stacked vertically and connected by thousands of short through-silicon vias, yielding far higher data throughput than conventional DDR memory at lower power. AI accelerators require HBM to feed their compute cores fast enough to keep utilization high; supply is dominated by SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics, and Micron Technology.

A chip-manufacturing technique that uses 13.5-nanometer extreme ultraviolet light to print transistor patterns smaller than 7nm on silicon wafers. The light is generated by firing CO₂ lasers at tin droplets 50,000 times per second; ASML is the sole commercial supplier of EUV systems worldwide, making it the deepest single-source dependency in the entire semiconductor supply chain.

The industry-standard substrate diameter for leading-edge semiconductor fabrication. Larger wafers yield more chips per production run, reducing unit cost; all advanced AI processors at sub-7nm nodes are fabricated exclusively on 300mm wafers. Shin-Etsu Chemical and SUMCO together supply roughly 55% of global 300mm wafer output.

Post-fabrication techniques — including CoWoS, fan-out wafer-level packaging, and 3D die stacking — that integrate multiple chips or memory dies into a single module with far shorter interconnects than a conventional circuit board. Advanced packaging has become a primary performance lever for AI chips because raw transistor shrinkage alone can no longer keep pace with compute demand.

article.fact_check: The chart assigns AI revenue percentages in the 6–10% range to raw-material companies such as Sibanye-Stillwater and Sumitomo Metal Mining. None of these companies disclose AI-specific revenue as a financial segment in their filings; the percentages appear to be the author's own estimates based on indirect downstream exposure. Whether palladium, nickel, or even lithium qualifies meaningfully as 'AI revenue' is contestable — the connection runs through two or more intermediate supply-chain steps. More significantly, the visualization's emphasis on raw materials and silicon wafers as primary bottleneck layers conflicts with independent analysis: Epoch AI's 2025 supply-chain study identified CoWoS advanced packaging (a TSMC-exclusive process) and high-bandwidth memory as the dominant constraints on AI chip production volume in 2025 — neither receives adequate weight in the chart as captured. The visualization maps real companies but may be optimizing for supply-chain breadth and investability over bottleneck severity.

ticker_msft.name: Microsoft Corporation
ticker_msft.description: Microsoft is a global software, cloud, and AI platform company. Its principal segments are Productivity and Business Processes (Office, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server products), and More Personal Computing (Windows, Xbox, Surface). The company is in a structural transition from a capital-light software licensor to a capital-intensive hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure provider.
ticker_msft.blurb: Microsoft is a global software, cloud, and AI platform company. Its principal segments are Productivity and Business Processes (Office, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server products), and More Personal Computing (Windows, Xbox, Surface). The company is in a structural transition from a capital-light software licensor to a capital-intensive hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure provider.
ticker_msft.recent: As of early May 2026, MSFT trades near $413 — down approximately 25.6% from its July 31, 2025 all-time high of $555.45 and -15.7% YTD — after touching a March 28 correction low of $356.07. The drawdown carried the stock briefly below its 200-week moving average for the first time in roughly 13 years (prior touches: 2009, 2018, 2020, 2022). Revenue grew 18% YoY with Azure +40%, while annualized AI revenue reached approximately $37 billion; calendar-2026 capex is projected near $190 billion and free cash flow contracted -22% YoY. Forward P/E is approximately 24.4.

ticker_mp.name: MP Materials Corp.
ticker_mp.blurb: MP Materials operates Mountain Pass in California, the only producing rare-earth mining and processing facility in the United States. The company extracts and refines neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide and in 2025 opened a full-scale permanent magnet manufacturing plant in Fort Worth, Texas. Its customers include General Motors under a long-term supply agreement for electric-vehicle traction motor magnets, and the U.S. government has backed the company with roughly $400 million in strategic investment.
ticker_mp.recent: In early 2025 MP Materials inaugurated its Fort Worth magnet facility and began commercial NdFeB magnet shipments to GM, a landmark for domestic rare-earth supply-chain independence. The company's AI revenue exposure remains indirect — data-center cooling fans and robotics actuators use its magnets — but the robotics angle is drawing increasing investor attention as humanoid robot programs scale.

ticker_alb.name: Albemarle Corporation
ticker_alb.blurb: Albemarle is one of the world's largest producers of lithium compounds, supplying battery-grade lithium hydroxide and carbonate to electric-vehicle and energy-storage markets. It also produces bromine and specialty chemicals. The company holds roughly 16% of global lithium market share and operates mines in Chile, Australia, and the United States. Its AI revenue exposure is indirect — lithium's primary demand driver remains EV batteries — but data-center battery backup systems and robotics batteries create a secondary link.
ticker_alb.recent: Albemarle has faced significant margin pressure through 2025 and into 2026 as lithium spot prices remained well below 2022 peaks amid a supply glut and slower-than-expected EV adoption in key markets. The company has responded by curtailing production and deferring expansion projects. AI-related demand for lithium is real but remains a small fraction of total consumption.

sources.title: Neodymium Market Size & Share | Grand View Research

ticker_fcx.name: Freeport-McMoRan Inc.
ticker_fcx.blurb: Freeport-McMoRan is the world's largest publicly traded copper producer, operating the Grasberg mine in Indonesia — one of the largest copper and gold deposits on Earth — alongside mines in North and South America. Copper is a critical input for data-center power infrastructure, server busbars, and the high-bandwidth interconnects inside AI rack systems. Freeport commands roughly 12% of global copper production and is essentially a leveraged bet on global electrification.
ticker_fcx.recent: Copper demand from AI data-center construction has become a notable demand driver alongside traditional grid and EV cable use, though Freeport's copper-to-AI revenue linkage remains indirect and diffuse. The company reported strong operational results through 2025, though it faces ongoing cost inflation at Grasberg. AI-related copper demand, while real, represents a relatively small share of total copper consumption today.

sources.title: Semiconductors in 2026: The AI-Driven Upswing Meets Structural Bottlenecks — Medium

ticker_spgi.name: S&P Global Inc.
ticker_spgi.blurb: S&P Global Inc. is a leading provider of financial intelligence, credit ratings, benchmarks, and analytics. Its core divisions include S&P Global Ratings (one of the world's three major credit rating agencies), S&P Global Market Intelligence (data and research platforms), S&P Global Commodity Insights, and S&P Dow Jones Indices, which administers the S&P 500 and thousands of other indices. The company significantly expanded its scale through the 2022 merger with IHS Markit, reinforcing its position as a critical infrastructure provider for global capital markets.
ticker_spgi.recent: Shares fell approximately 4.15% on May 13, 2026, closing at $406.55 — a notable single-day decline that prompted coverage on MarketBeat asking why the stock dropped, though the specific catalyst is not detailed in available sources. Pre-market pricing on May 14 showed a modest recovery to $407.97, suggesting the sell-off may be stabilizing. Not enough public information from these sources to confirm the precise earnings or macro trigger behind the move.

ticker_4063-t.name: Shin-Etsu Chemical Co., Ltd.
ticker_4063-t.blurb: Shin-Etsu Chemical is a Japanese diversified chemical conglomerate and one of the world's largest chemical companies by market capitalization. Its two dominant businesses are polyvinyl chloride (PVC), where it holds the global number-one position, and semiconductor silicon wafers, where it is likewise the world's leading supplier. The company also produces silicones, rare-earth magnets, and cellulose derivatives, serving industries ranging from construction and electronics to automotive and pharmaceuticals. Its consistent profitability and conservative balance sheet have made it a benchmark blue-chip within Japanese equities.

ticker_3436-t.name: Sumco Corporation
ticker_3436-t.blurb: Sumco Corporation is a Japanese semiconductor materials company that manufactures and sells silicon wafers used in chip fabrication. Its product portfolio spans polished, annealed, epitaxial, junction-isolated, silicon-on-insulator, and reclaimed polished wafers, as well as monocrystalline ingots. The company operates globally across Japan, the United States, China, Taiwan, South Korea, and Europe. Formerly known as Sumitomo Mitsubishi Silicon Corp., it rebranded as Sumco in August 2005 and is headquartered in Minato, Tokyo.
ticker_3436-t.recent: Sumco reported earnings on May 12, 2026, with trailing twelve-month net income remaining negative at -¥23.27B and EPS of -¥66.53, reflecting continued softness in the silicon wafer market. Morningstar noted that forward guidance remains weak but raised its fair value estimate to ¥1,440, signaling an upbeat longer-term outlook. The stock has surged roughly 241% over the past year, trading around ¥3,427 on May 14, 2026, with a 52-week range of ¥937–¥3,859.

ticker_3037-tw.blurb: Unimicron Technology Corp. is a Taiwan-based manufacturer of printed circuit boards (PCBs) and IC substrates, serving the semiconductor and electronics industries. The company is a key supplier for advanced packaging solutions, including substrates for high-performance computing and AI chips. It holds a strong market position as one of the world's largest IC substrate producers, competing with companies like Ibiden and Shinko Electric Industries.

The company reported steady revenue growth, supported by robust demand for ABF substrates used in AI and data center applications. Analysts have highlighted its potential to benefit from increased chip packaging complexity, though near-term price action has been mixed amid global economic uncertainties.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_tsm.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company
ticker_tsm.blurb: TSMC is the world's largest contract chipmaker, fabricating semiconductors designed by Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and dozens of others. It controls roughly 60% of global foundry revenue and an even higher share of advanced-node manufacturing (3nm and below). TSMC's competitive position rests on process technology leadership, enormous capital expenditure scale, and a customer base that has no viable alternative at leading-edge geometries. Its Taiwanese concentration is the central geopolitical risk that market participants perpetually discount, then rediscover.
ticker_tsm.recent: TSMC reported Q1 2026 revenue of approximately NT$839 billion (roughly $26 billion USD), up around 41% year-over-year, driven by surging AI accelerator demand from Nvidia and Apple. The company's CoWoS advanced packaging capacity — critical for HBM memory integration in AI GPUs — remains sold out through at least 2026. TSMC appeared on Palantir's Q1 2026 Rule of 80 Frontier chart with a composite growth-plus-margin score of 88%, placing it fourth among large-cap companies on that metric.

ticker_mu.name: Micron Technology, Inc.
ticker_mu.blurb: Micron is the only US-headquartered manufacturer of DRAM and NAND memory at scale, competing with Samsung and SK Hynix. Historically the most cyclical of the three, it has spent the past two years repositioning toward high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked DRAM that pairs with AI accelerators, where pricing is multiples of standard DDR5 and contracts are multi-year rather than spot.
ticker_mu.recent: In March 2026 Micron began mass production of HBM4 12-Hi 36GB stacks for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform; management has stated 2026 HBM capacity is sold out under binding agreements. Fiscal Q2 2026 revenue was around $23.9 billion, with non-GAAP gross margin near 75%. The board approved a 30% dividend increase and roughly $25 billion of fiscal-2026 capex. Despite a strong year-to-date move, the forward P/E remains in the high single digits on consensus, reflecting residual cyclicality scepticism.

ticker_asml.name: ASML Holding N.V.
ticker_asml.blurb: ASML is a Dutch semiconductor equipment company and the sole manufacturer of EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography machines — the tools required to print the finest circuit features on leading-edge chips at 5nm and below. Every AI accelerator, high-bandwidth memory chip, and advanced logic die manufactured at TSMC, Samsung, or Intel passes through ASML optics. The company's monopoly position emerged after decades of public-private R&D investment in partnership with European governments and chipmakers.
ticker_asml.recent: ASML reported €32.7 billion in total net sales for full-year 2025, up roughly 16% year-on-year, with net income of €9.6 billion and a gross margin of 52.8%. Year-end backlog stood at €38.8 billion. Q4 2025 saw record total net sales of €9.7 billion, including revenue recognized for the first High-NA EUV systems — the next-generation machines required for 2nm nodes and below. TSMC accounts for an estimated 40% of EUV tool deliveries. ASML guides to €34–39 billion for 2026 and €44–60 billion by 2030 as High-NA adoption widens. In December 2025 Huawei and Chinese startup SiCarrier confirmed a functional EUV light source using an alternative plasma architecture, but analysts place production-ready Chinese competition no earlier than 2028–2030.
